query: For high-entropy alloys intended as intermediate materials in plasma-facing reactor components, what single intervention could improve heat-transfer capability while preserving structural integrity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the expected outcome compared with current intermediate-layer performance, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Subjecting a cast, refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) to a controlled liquid metal infiltration process with molten Cu will induce a phase‐separated, bicontinuous microstructure composed of a continuous, high-conductivity FCC Cu network embedded in a stable refractory BCC HEA matrix. This engineered architecture is expected to boost the heat-transfer capability by enhancing electronic and lattice thermal transport while preserving the overall structural integrity under high temperature and irradiation conditions encountered in plasma‐facing reactor components.
generation.material_initial_state: A cast, single-phase refractory HEA exhibiting a homogeneous BCC microstructure typically used as an intermediate layer in plasma-facing components (e.g., a nominally equiatomic CrMoNbTa or similar composition).
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA preform to molten Cu under controlled conditions (e.g., infiltrate with Cu at approximately 1000 °C for 2–4 hours in an inert atmosphere) to promote selective liquid metal infiltration and phase separation.
generation.conditions: The processing intervention is carried out at around 1000 °C for a few hours under an inert or vacuum environment. The resulting structure is intended to perform under service conditions with thermal cycling from room temperature to ~800 °C and moderate He+ irradiation mimicking plasma exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: A bicontinuous, co-continuous microstructure featuring interconnected FCC Cu channels that form within and along the HEA matrix, with limited interfacial reaction layers that maintain strong bonding between phases.
generation.mechanism: Due to differences in mixing enthalpies, the molten Cu selectively infiltrates and segregates within the HEA, forming a continuous, high conductivity network. This network augments overall heat transfer via enhanced electronic and lattice transport, while the remaining refractory HEA provides mechanical strength and resistance to irradiation-induced swelling. The controlled infiltration avoids deleterious reactions that could compromise structural integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated, monolithic HEA, the infiltrated composite should exhibit a substantial increase (potentially on the order of 50–100% improvement) in thermal conductivity while retaining comparable mechanical strength and resistance to irradiation-induced damage under thermal cycling up to ~800 °C.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the untreated, single-phase refractory HEA that currently offers lower thermal conductivity and a uniform microstructure without dedicated heat-transfer channels.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective when performed under controlled infiltration conditions (≈1000 °C, 2–4 hours) and validated under service temperatures up to ~800 °C with moderate energetic He+ exposure. The approach may not hold under significantly higher irradiation doses, extended thermal exposures beyond 800 °C, or if the interfacial bonding between Cu and HEA is degraded during long-term operation.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise magnitude of thermal conductivity improvement and the long-term stability of the bicontinuous microstructure, especially under prolonged cyclic thermal and irradiation conditions. The balance between enhanced conduction and potential embrittlement due to phase segregation also remains to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one group of the base HEA and another group processed by Cu infiltration under the specified conditions. Characterize the microstructure using SEM/TEM with EDS mapping to verify the formation of interpenetrating Cu channels and the integrity of the HEA matrix. Measure thermal conductivity using laser flash analysis and evaluate mechanical strength using nanoindentation and cyclic thermal loading tests. Finally, subject both sample sets to controlled He+ irradiation and monitor changes in microstructure (via AFM and TEM) and thermal as well as mechanical performance.
measurements: SEM/TEM with EDS for microstructural and interfacial characterization
Laser flash analysis for temperature-dependent thermal conductivity
Nanoindentation and cyclic thermal tests for mechanical properties
AFM/TEM after He+ irradiation for assessing irradiation-induced swelling or blistering
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu-infiltrated HEA samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant (≥50%) improvement in thermal conductivity relative to the untreated HEA, or if they exhibit mechanical degradation or enhanced irradiation damage compared to the baseline, the hypothesis will be rejected.
